sources.citation: ELAR deposit nawuri-dakubu-0325, 'Vanishing Voices from Ghana's middle belt' (Mary Esther Kropp Dakubu, 2012-2013).
sources.note: Deposit languages: Nawuri, Kiliji, Yoruba, Gonja, English; 20 bundles (Balai clan, Kiliji songs, blacksmithing, guinea-corn festival, 'Linguistic data'..). No bundle concerns Ntrapo/Nterato or Kpalangase; the 2007 77-word Ntrapo list is not listed.

sources.note: No article, thesis, sketch or wordlist publication on Nterato/Ntrapo found anywhere; archive.org full-text hits are scanned noise or the unrelated Nchumuru/Banda clan-quarter name 'Ntrapo' in Agorsah's archaeology.

sources.citation: Kropp Dakubu, Mary Esther. 2013. PROJECT REPORT: Research on Vanishing Languages and Practices in the Northern Guang Area in Ghana: a preliminary report. Ghana Journal of Linguistics 2(1): 79-86. (Glottolog ref 317133)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Nterato/Ntrapo occupies one paragraph (p.79 + fn.1): in 2007 two elderly men at Kpalangase still spoke the language Goody (1963) called Nterato, calling it Ntrapo; a 77-word list merged with Goody's 42 words 'confirmed that this is a north Guang language, similar to but not identical with several other languages of the area'; endonym ntrapʊ (sg bədrapʊ, pl ntrapʊna); p.82 notes a plural suffix -na. The rest of the report is about the Yoruba cult language Kiliji and Balai prayer language. No phonology, no tone or stress statement.

sources.citation: Kropp Dakubu, M. E. & S. A. Ntewusu. 2007. Unpublished Kpalangase field notes: 77-word Ntrapo list (merged with Goody's 42 words), collected during a trip between Tamale and Salaga.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Largest lexical record of the language (77 words, sound recordings implied); the only material from which a native-speaker prosodic pattern could ever be checked. Not published; not listed in the ELAR 'Vanishing Voices' deposit — may survive in Kropp Dakubu's papers at the Institute of African Studies, Legon.
